title: The Pastry Makers Who Planned Bimbo After Ten at Night
dek: From 1943 to 1945 Lorenzo Servitje and his partners planned a packaged-bread factory in Mexico City, admitting what they did not know and borrowing the rest.

story.founder: Lorenzo Servitje, Jaime Sendra, Alfonso Velasco, Jaime Jorba, José T. Mata, Roberto Servitje
story.event: Planning and opening a packaged-bread factory in Mexico City
story.summary: Lorenzo Servitje, who had run his late father's Mexico City pastry shop El Molino since he was eighteen, spent 1943 to 1945 planning an industrial bakery with his uncle Jaime Sendra, the engineer Alfonso Velasco, Jaime Jorba and José T. Mata. Panificación Bimbo opened on 2 December 1945 with American machinery ordered under wartime restrictions, cellophane-wrapped bread and ten delivery vehicles, and by Servitje's account reached its target of a million pesos in annual sales by the end of 1946.
paragraphs: Between 1943 and 1945, after ten at night, Lorenzo Servitje met his partners at his home to plan a bread factory. El Molino was the Mexico City pastry shop his father had founded; Lorenzo had run it since his father's sudden death, when he was eighteen and had hoped to become a writer or historian. He had also been reading American trade magazines about industrial baking. His uncle Jaime Sendra, El Molino's production chief, put the question to him: why not start a bakery? By his own account, Servitje said yes without thinking.

What they lacked was know-how. Sendra took a baking course by correspondence, but it could not teach industrial production, so they brought in Alfonso Velasco, an engineer fourteen years older than Servitje, trained at a leading American baking school, who had worked as a technician for the competitor Pan Ideal. Servitje later described himself and his partners as simple pastry makers with good will, and Velasco as the expert. Velasco became the technical partner, paid in a share of profits rather than capital; Jaime Jorba took sales; Sendra and José T. Mata put in money; Servitje was general manager.

They planned for an investment of a million pesos but had roughly 375,000, so they sought a 500,000-peso bank loan, and Servitje's father-in-law sold them land in Santa María Insurgentes payable in instalments. Wartime restrictions held up American machinery until May 1945, when suppliers began taking orders. Velasco knew Pan Ideal's weaknesses, paper wrapping and mouldy bread left on shelves, so the plan was for cellophane that let buyers see the loaf, collection of unsold bread after two days, and ten delivery vehicles where Pan Ideal had four, one or two of them former ambulances.

Panificación Bimbo opened on 2 December 1945, timed for the December season, selling Súper Pan Bimbo, black bread and toast. Velasco hired nineteen production workers; the company's own history counts thirty-four employees at the start. Servitje's brother Roberto, seventeen, joined as a supervisor. The partners had aimed for a million pesos in annual sales, and Servitje said they reached it by the end of 1946.

quote.text: Above all things, order, and distribution, and singling out of parts, is the life of dispatch; so as the distribution be not too subtle: for he that doth not divide, will never enter well into business; and he that divideth too much, will never come out of it clearly
quote.source_title: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral, Project Gutenberg eBook #575
quote.connection: Bacon was advising on how to handle business at a council table, but his rule fits a founding team. Bimbo's partners split the work cleanly: production to Velasco, sales to Jorba, money to Sendra and Mata, management to Servitje. Each knew which part was his to enter.

reflection: The most useful line in Servitje's account may be the one where he admits that he and his partners were pastry makers, not industrial bakers. Rather than pretend otherwise, they gave the expert his own part of the work and a share of what it earned, and each partner knew which part belonged to him.

You may be carrying pieces of your work that someone else could do better, out of habit or a sense that you ought to know everything yourself. Naming what you do not know is not a weakness. It is how work gets divided sensibly, and how some of it gets put down.
invitation: Pick one task on your list that someone you know understands better than you do. Ask them one specific question about it today, instead of working it out alone.

sources.supports: Largely in Lorenzo Servitje's own words: his father's sudden death when he was eighteen and his abandoned hopes of being a writer or historian; running El Molino; reading American trade magazines; Jaime Sendra's proposal and Servitje's quick yes; Sendra's correspondence course from the American Institute of Baking, which could not teach industrial production; Alfonso Velasco, fourteen years older, sent to a leading US baking school, previously Pan Ideal's technician; 'simples pasteleros con buena voluntad'; partners' roles and Velasco's profit share without capital; planning sessions at Servitje's home after 10 p.m. from 1943 to 1945; planned investment of one million pesos, about 375,000 available and a 500,000-peso bank loan sought; land in Santa María Insurgentes from his father-in-law in instalments; wartime machinery restrictions until May 1945; Pan Ideal's paper wrapping and mouldy bread; cellophane; collecting bread after two days; ten vehicles against Pan Ideal's four, one or two of them former ambulances; nineteen production workers; opening on 2 December 1945 for the December season; launch products; Roberto Servitje joining at seventeen as a supervisor; the million-peso sales target reached by the end of 1946.

cross_checks.claim: Jaime Sendra proposed the bakery to Lorenzo Servitje, who had run El Molino since his father's death
Alfonso Velasco supplied the industrial baking know-how the pastry-makers lacked
The bread was wrapped in cellophane so buyers could see its freshness
The factory was in Santa María Insurgentes, Mexico City

research_notes: The main source is an excerpt from Silvia Cherem's 2008 book on Bimbo's founders, published by Expansión and told largely in Lorenzo Servitje's own words; Servitje's remarks are in Spanish and are paraphrased, not quoted. Headcount differs: Cherem has Velasco hiring 19 production workers in November 1945; Grupo Bimbo's history and Forbes give 34 employees at the start (another outlet says 38); the story gives the 19 and the company's 34 with attribution. Capital: Cherem gives about 375,000 pesos available against a planned million, and elsewhere says the partners pooled about 300,000 from earlier businesses; the story says 'roughly 375,000'. Dates: Cherem says Juan Servitje died in 1936; Forbes says 1937 and Grupo Bimbo and El Financiero have Lorenzo running El Molino from 1937, so the story says only that he was eighteen. Cherem says Panificación Bimbo was incorporated before a notary on 4 July 1944; El Financiero gives 4 July 1945 as the founding; operations began on 2 December 1945 in all accounts, which the story uses. Founders: the company lists six including Roberto Servitje, who joined at seventeen as a supervisor; several outlets list five. Funding is marked bootstrapped: the partners' own savings plus a bank loan and loans from relatives (one, José Torrallardona, took 10 per cent equity); there were no outside investors. The Bacon passage concerns ordering the parts of business in deliberation; it is applied by analogy to a division of roles. Essay numbering follows the 1625 edition ('Of Dispatch' is Essay 25).
